newsitem.title: SPAIN: GOLF-UNHERALDED SUNESON MOUNTS MASTERS CHALLENGE.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-UNHERALDED SUNESON MOUNTS MASTERS CHALLENGE.

text.p: Carl Suneson, a stranger to the European Tour leader boards, has been learning to cope with diabetes since June last year.
It was then that he learned that wild fluctuations in his form stemmed from variations in his blood sugar level because of the condition.
Now Suneson is dealing with it successfully his form has levelled out and he enters Saturday's third round of the Volvo Masters at Valderrama sharing third place.
Suneson, who plays under Spanish nationality, is three behind Britain's Paul Curry, two back from Trinidad's Stephen Ames and equal with Andy Oldcorn, another Briton.

He described the discovery last year that he had diabetes as "almost my downfall". "I lost weight and also discovered I had a thyroid condition which together with the diabetes was affecting my metabolism."
He monitors his blood sugar four times a day, after each meal and before he goes to bed, and eats four or five bananas during every round.
"Golf is a good sport for diabetics because it burns your blood sugar very slowly," he said. "With other sports, it burns very quickly."
Suneson, now Spanish, is half Swedish, half English. His father went to England as a young man to learn the language, married the daughter of the family he was staying with and returned to Sweden.
They went to the Spanish-owned Canary Islands on holiday and stayed, his father opening a restaurant at Maspalomas on the island of Gran Canaria.

Suneson was born there and is now married to a Spanish girl. "But because my mother was English I was able to keep English citizenship because if I adopted Spanish nationality I would be eligible for national service.
"Now I have a son, I am exempt," he said. "So I decided it was time to play for Spain."
He lost his European Tour playing card last year for the second year running but was successful in the qualifying school.
"This year my aim was to keep my card," said Suneson, who entered the Masters 53rd on the money list after some strong performances early and late in the season.
"Up to last year I would play well one day and shoot 80 the next and I didn't know why. It turned out my blood sugar count was low and my concentration was bad," he said.
"Now I am a more consistent player."
